Limestone. A sedimentary rock composed primarily of calcium carbonate, typically formed from the skeletal material and shells of marine organisms. It's abundant in shallow marine deposits and forms cliffs, caves, and karst landscapes. Limestone is economically important as a construction material, as aggregate, and as a source of lime—calcium oxide—for cement and steel production.

Limestone forms in shallow marine environments from the accumulation of shell fragments, skeletal debris, and inorganic carbonate precipitation. It's composed almost entirely of calcite, and you can often see fossil shells, corals, and foraminifera with the naked eye. One of the definitive field tests is that it fizzes vigorously when exposed to dilute hydrochloric acid, which confirms the presence of carbonate minerals.

Limestone is light-coloured—typically white, cream, grey, or tan—due to its pure carbonate composition and lack of iron. It's soluble in slightly acidic water, which leads to karst topography with sinkholes, caves, underground streams, and dramatic cliff formations. When limestone is buried and heated, it metamorphoses to marble, which is harder and denser due to the recrystallisation of calcite.

Calcite is the primary mineral component of limestone. Marble is the metamorphic rock formed from limestone buried and heated. Limestone is the quintessential biochemical sedimentary rock, formed from organism activity. And limestone preserves fossils abundantly because shells and skeletal material accumulate on the seafloor, making it an invaluable record of ancient life.
